sentences.show: In November 1942, in just four days, the Red Army surrounded about 300,000 Axis soldiers, on the frozen steppe beside the Volga.
Many historians call it the greatest defeat in the history of the German Army.
And it was built on a trick Hannibal made famous at Cannae: the pincer.
In the summer of 1942, Germany launched a new offensive in the south of the Soviet Union. It was called Case Blue.
Hitler split his forces. One half went for the oil of the Caucasus. The other, the Sixth Army, went for Stalingrad.
The city carried Stalin’s name. That alone made it a prize.
For three months, the Germans fought for it, street by street, house by house.
The Soviet commander, Chuikov, ordered his men to hug the enemy, to stay so close that German planes and artillery could not hit them without hitting their own men.
Pavlov’s House, a four-story building, was held by a single platoon for weeks.
One division lost 30 percent of its men in the first 24 hours. Of 10,000, only 320 were left at the end.
By November, the Germans held 90 percent of the ruined city, and had pinned the defenders against the Volga.
But the Germans had a weakness. And the Soviets knew exactly where.
The long flanks of the Sixth Army, north and south of the city, were guarded not by Germans, but by Romanian armies.
Poorly equipped. Old guns, horse-drawn artillery, and tanks whose small guns could not hurt a Soviet T-34.
Hitler trusted them anyway.
Stalin’s generals saw the weakness, and built a plan on it. Operation Uranus.
They gathered about 1.1 million men, 800 tanks, and 13,000 guns.
And they hid it. Radio silence. Camouflage. Orders carried by couriers instead of radio.
In three weeks, they ferried 111,000 soldiers, and hundreds of tanks, across the Volga.
The Germans suspected an attack. But they did not know where, or when.
On 19 November, in the fog, the northern pincer struck the Third Romanian Army.
The Romanians held for a few hours, then collapsed. By the end of the day, 27,000 were prisoners.
The next day, the southern pincer broke through the Fourth Romanian Army.
Two arrows, aimed at one place: the town of Kalach, on the river Don, behind the Sixth Army.
On 23 November, Soviet tanks from the north met Soviet tanks from the south.
At first, they mistook each other for Germans, and traded fire.
The ring was closed. Inside it, between 250,000 and 330,000 men. Estimates differ.
The link-up had not been filmed. So the Soviets staged it again, for the newsreels.
Hitler refused to let the Sixth Army break out. It would be supplied from the air.
The airlift needed 750 tons a day. It delivered 105.
Field Marshal Manstein tried to break in from the outside. He got within 48 kilometers. But the starving Sixth Army never broke out to meet him.
On 2 February, 1943, the last pocket surrendered.
About 91,000 exhausted, starving men were taken prisoner, among them 22 generals.
Days earlier, Göring had compared the trapped army to the 300 Spartans at Thermopylae. The soldiers did not appreciate it.
The total cost is still debated. Axis casualties: from 800,000 to 1.5 million, depending on the source.
Soviet casualties: more than 1 million, by official figures. Some historians say that is too low.
More than a million soldiers and civilians may have died. It is one of the bloodiest battles in history.
The myth of the invincible German army was gone. In the Soviet Union, they said: you cannot stop an army that has done Stalingrad.
More than two thousand years after Cannae, the pincer had won again. Different armies. Same lesson. Guard only your front, and you will be hit on the flanks.
So, was Stalingrad won in the ruined streets, or on the open steppe, on the flanks? Tell us what you think.
The Red Army closed a pincer. You can close one too, on the subscribe button.
